messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: good news
parts:
I got the 8 schools working (pretty much, if not perfect) by randomizing epsilon and L at each step. Not to stop periodicity but to allow HMC to get stuck from places where big steps or long chains will invariably get rejected. Currently I'm setting epsilon and L independent:
epsilon <- runif (1, 0, 2*epsilon.0)
L <- ceiling (2*L.0*runif(1))
But now I'm thinking it could be logical to have them be positively correlated.

On Jul 21, 2012, at 11:24 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> On 7/21/12 3:44 AM, Andrew Gelman wrote:> I got the 8 schools working (pretty much, if not perfect) by randomizing epsilon and L at each step.
> > Not to stop periodicity but to allow HMC to get stuck from places where big steps or long
> > chains will invariably get rejected.
>
> What I don't understand is that there's almost no
> rejection.

What happens is that in the constrained parameter version (sigma unlogged, no bouncing), the chains go off to negative sigma -> rejection.
When I tried unlogged sigma _with_ bouncing, the chains, if they ever got near zero, would get ricocheted off to huge values of sigma -> rejection. The problem arose because of huge gradients on sigma.
When I tried log sigma, the chains would again sometimes go to extreme values.

The only way to avoid rejection was with tiny step sizes, and then there was no mixing.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] good news (8 schools HMC)
parts:
On Jul 22, 2012, at 2:50 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> So you get a huge gradient toward 0 (?) and then a big
> bounce? I'd have thought that as sigma approaches 0,
> the total gradient would push away from 0 unless the
> coefficients were all very tightly clustered.
>
> Maybe Michael can explain how he gets it to work.

Yeah, it sounds like there's not enough data to temper the prior and you're essentially trying to sample from 1/\sigma.

What isn't clear to me is why you're getting such extreme ricochets. As you approach zero from positive values the gradients increase, which increases the momenta. When you finally bounce, then, the reflected momenta will be large. But as you continue back through positive values the gradients should temper that momentum -- modulo the small epsilon you move past the origin the evolution should be symmetric with p -> -p. So unless you started at huge values of sigma I'm not sure how you're able to bounce to them.

Have you checked that the magnitude of the momenta along sigma is equal before and after the bounce?

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] good news (8 schools HMC)
parts: See below.

On Jul 22, 2012, at 8:50 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

>> What happens is that in the constrained parameter version (sigma unlogged, no bouncing), the chains go off to negative sigma -> rejection.
>
> Right -- Stan would probably do that, too, if you don't
> declare the variable properly. Another thing we might
> want to try to catch and diagnose automatically.
Yes, but Stan with Nuts should still work sorta ok in such situations.

>
>> When I tried unlogged sigma _with_ bouncing, the chains, if they ever got near zero, would get ricocheted off to huge values of sigma -> rejection.
>
> > The problem arose because of huge gradients on sigma.
>
> So you get a huge gradient toward 0 (?) and then a big
> bounce? I'd have thought that as sigma approaches 0,
> the total gradient would push away from 0 unless the
> coefficients were all very tightly clustered.

What happens is that when sigma is near zero, d(log p)/d(sigma) gets huge. Without bouncing, this sends HMC off to big negative values and rejection. With bouncing, it sends HMC off to big positive values. The problem is the persistence of the momentum variable. It goes like this: sigma is 0.6, say, and then the gradient is huge, then the momentum is huge, then it gets bounced off to sigma = 50 or so, now the gradient is negative but small, so it takes a long long long time for the momentum to get back negative. In the meantime, sigma becomes more and more extreme.

>
>> The only way to avoid rejection was with tiny step sizes, and then there was no mixing.
>
> I was able to run small step sizes and long chains and get
> mixing that was good enough to satisfy R-hat on multiple
> chains from diffuse starting points.
>
Yes, I got that too (with log sigma) but then I was getting 99-100% accept rates, which didn't make me so happy.  I preferred the results with random epsilon and L at each step.

parts:
M
I don't understand the question. When I bounce, I simply set sigma <- - sigma and momentum(sigma) <- - momentum (sigma). Here's the R code below. Do I have a mistake? Here, "th" is the vector of 10 parameters (sigma is theta[10]) and "phi" is momentum.
A

hmc.iteration <- function (th, y, s.y, L, epsilon, M){
d <- length (th)
phi <- rnorm (d, 0, 1)
th.old <- th
log.p.old <- log.p.th (th,y,s.y) - 0.5*sum(phi^2)
phi <- phi + 0.5*epsilon*gradient.th (th, y, s.y)
for (l in 1:L){
th <- th + epsilon*phi
if (th[10] < 0) {
th[10] <- - th[10]
phi[10] <- - phi[10]
}
phi <- phi + (if (l==L) 0.5 else 1)*epsilon*gradient.th (th, y, s.y)
}
phi <- -phi
log.p.star <- log.p.th (th,y,s.y) - 0.5*sum(phi^2)
r <- exp (log.p.star - log.p.old)
if (is.nan(r)) r <- 0
p.jump <- min(r,1)
th.new <- if (runif(1) < p.jump) th else th.old
return (list (th=th.new, p.jump=p.jump))

}

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] good news (8 schools HMC)
parts:
On Jul 22, 2012, at 3:15 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:

> What happens is that when sigma is near zero, d(log p)/d(sigma) gets huge. Without bouncing, this sends HMC off to big negative values and rejection. With bouncing, it sends HMC off to big positive values. The problem is the persistence of the momentum variable. It goes like this: sigma is 0.6, say, and then the gradient is huge, then the momentum is huge, then it gets bounced off to sigma = 50 or so, now the gradient is negative but small, so it takes a long long long time for the momentum to get back negative. In the meantime, sigma becomes more and more extreme.

Oh, oh, oh. Are you bouncing right before you violate the constraint or afterwards? You want to bounce as soon as you're in violation of the constraint (the first time the spatial update passes q = 0) but not before that. As I mentioned in my response to Bob, you should be seeing roughly symmetry bounces and not huge jumps into regions in which you have not yet been.

See Algo 1 (page 13) here: http://arxiv.org/pdf/1005.0157.pdf. In this case C(x) = x and (grad C / | gradC |) = 1.

>> if (th[10] < 0) {
>> th[10] <- - th[10]
>> phi[10] <- - phi[10]
>> }
>> phi <- phi + (if (l==L) 0.5 else 1)*epsilon*gradient.th (th, y, s.y)
>> }
>> phi <- -phi
>>
>>
>> Are you saying that if I just eliminate the line, "th[10] <- - th[10]", then I'm ok? So it's alright that I first move theta to the illegal zone, then I flip the sign of phi, then I update phi? The difficulty here is that my update is based on the gradient of the updated (negative) theta. Is this right?

It goes like this: sigma is 0.6, say, and then the gradient is huge, then the momentum is huge, then it gets bounced off to sigma = 50 or so, now the gradient is negative but small, so it takes a long long long time for the momentum to get back negative. In the meantime, sigma becomes more and more extreme.

>>>> Oh, oh, oh. Are you bouncing right before you violate the constraint or afterwards? You want to bounce as soon as you're in violation of the constraint (the first time the spatial update passes q = 0) but not before that. As I mentioned in my response to Bob, you should be seeing roughly symmetry bounces and not huge jumps into regions in which you have not yet been.

>>>> See Algo 1 (page 13) here: http://arxiv.org/pdf/1005.0157.pdf. In this case C(x) = x and (grad C / | gradC |) = 1.
>>
